Most people probably have only a patchy idea of what biomedical ultrasound is and what it is used for, yet almost everyone will run into it at some point in their lives. Why? Because the ultrasound scan, which people in China simply call a “B-scan” after B-mode ultrasound, belongs to biomedical ultrasound. Mention an ultrasound scan and I bet nearly everyone goes “Oh, right,” because they’ve had one. It is, after all, a standard part of routine checkups and of the workup for many diseases.

Figure 1. An ultrasound scan

(http://www.kangailu.com/a/201512/unews-10283.html)

Figure 2. Medical ultrasound coupling gel (we blurred the logo so this doesn’t look like an ad; apologies, and we will remove the image on request)

Since we’re on the subject of ultrasound scans, let’s start with two fun things about them.

The first: every time you have an abdominal scan, once you lie down, the doctor smears a large dollop of cold, sticky, gooey liquid on your belly. This stuff is called medical ultrasound coupling gel, and it looks like Figure 2. Once it’s on, your tummy actually feels rather nice, almost liberating. But before you can enjoy it, the doctor starts pressing the ultrasound probe hard into your belly, again and again. (So ticklish! No, I must keep my dignity and hold it in.) The whole exam goes back and forth a few times between more gel and more probe-pressing, which is quite the bittersweet experience. And before you’ve had your fill of it, the exam is over: you hop up, wipe off the gel, and the next patient lies down.

Figure 3. The ultrasound experience

The second: physical checkups often include an ultrasound of the prostate. Beforehand, the doctor always tells everyone to drink water and hold their urine, or they won’t be scanned. Yet people often decide they’ve drunk about enough and held it long enough, trot over to the doctor full of hope, and get sent back with “Not yet. Keep drinking, keep holding, come back later.” The rule for holding it is that the urine should fill the entire prostate as far as possible. At last you’re full enough and the doctor is satisfied, though you’re a little scared the probe will squeeze the urine right out of you (just kidding, that doesn’t normally happen). Once the scan is over, off you rush to the toilet for some relief.

Figure 4. Normally, when you need to go, don’t hold it in. But for a prostate ultrasound, hold it you must.

So here’s the question: what is behind these two ultrasound rituals? To make it easier to understand, let’s start with a simple analogy. As in Figure 5, suppose we need to get from the orange area to the green area. If there is a huge drop between them, as on the left of Figure 5, it is terrifying: nobody would dare jump, and we’d just have to turn back. But if the two areas are at nearly the same height, as on the right, it’s a piece of cake and we can hop across with ease.

Ultrasound propagation works in a similar way. It’s just that what decides whether a person jumps becomes, for an ultrasound wave, the “characteristic impedance.” Don’t worry about what characteristic impedance is just yet; we’ll explain it below. For now, just remember that applying gel or holding your urine both serve to shrink the gap in characteristic impedance (like the height difference between the orange and green areas in Figure 5), so that the ultrasound waves can get into the body more easily and the scan works better.

Figure 5. To jump or not to jump?

So how do we explain these two phenomena scientifically? It comes down to the transmission of ultrasound. Since this article doesn’t want to go too deep into acoustic theory, we will use only the simplest case, a plane wave at normal incidence on the boundary between two media. Figure 6 shows how a plane wave is reflected and transmitted at the interface. When a plane wave pi traveling in medium 1 (density ρ1, sound speed c1) hits medium 2 (density ρ2, sound speed c2) head-on, only part of it crosses the interface into medium 2 as the transmitted wave pt. The rest is reflected back at the interface as the reflected wave pr. Acoustic theory gives the intensity (energy flux density) transmission coefficient tI for a plane wave at normal incidence on two media, that is, the ratio of the sound energy transmitted into medium 2 to the incident energy in medium 1, as:

(1)

where Z1 = ρ1c1 and Z2 = ρ2c2 are the characteristic impedances of media 1 and 2. (Pay attention, class: this is what “characteristic impedance” means!)

Figure 6. Reflection and transmission of a plane wave at an interface

Now we can use Equation (1) to see what happens to the ultrasound if no gel is applied or the patient doesn’t hold their urine. In that case, in the model of Figure 6, medium 2 is air in both examples. (Note: if the probe touches the skin directly, there is inevitably some air in between; and if the prostate isn’t filled with urine, there will also be air.) Medium 1 is the piezoelectric material (strictly speaking, the matching layer, which we won’t go into here) or the soft tissue of the body, respectively. For air we can take the usual values of density and sound speed, ρ = 1.29 kg/m³ and c = 340 m/s. The density and sound speed of piezoelectric materials and soft tissue are greater than or comparable to those of water, so for simplicity we use the usual values for water, ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and c = 1500 m/s. Without gel or a full bladder, the intensity transmission coefficient of the ultrasound during the scan is then:

As you can see, the ultrasound can hardly get into the tissue or the region of the prostate being examined. And if no ultrasound reaches the tissue or the prostate, there is no scan to speak of. Figure 7 plots the intensity transmission coefficient against the characteristic impedance of medium 2, with the impedance of the incident medium 1 held constant (here, the characteristic impedance of water). Figure 7 shows that the transmission coefficient approaches 1 only as the impedance of medium 2 approaches that of medium 1, that is, only then can the incident wave pass efficiently from medium 1 into medium 2.

So the reason for applying gel or holding your urine before an ultrasound scan is to replace the air in medium 2 with gel or urine, whose characteristic impedance is much closer to that of medium 1. That boosts the transmission of the ultrasound, gives better image quality and makes for a better exam.

Figure 7. Intensity transmission coefficient as a function of the characteristic impedance of medium 2, with the characteristic impedance of incident medium 1 held constant

That was a little background on ultrasound scans. I hope it has given you a rough picture of ultrasound scanning, and even of biomedical ultrasound in general.

The next part gives an overview of biomedical ultrasound and how its systems are classified.

Biomedical ultrasound: an overview

Biomedical ultrasonics is an interdisciplinary field that combines acoustics (a branch of physics) with electronic and information engineering, materials science, biomedicine and other disciplines.

People often confuse medical ultrasound with ultrasound medicine and can’t tell them apart. In fact, biomedical ultrasonics is different from ultrasound medicine. The former studies how ultrasound propagates in biological tissue and puts that knowledge to use for medical diagnosis and treatment. The latter studies clinical diagnostic methods that use ultrasound.

The theory of vibrations, waves and fields is the foundation of biomedical ultrasonics, which comprises two branches: medical ultrasound physics and medical ultrasound engineering. Medical ultrasound physics studies how ultrasound propagates in biological tissue. Medical ultrasound engineering applies those laws of propagation to design and build ultrasound equipment for diagnosis and treatment. Modern medical ultrasound systems and devices bring acoustic theory into medicine through the advanced technology of ever-developing fields such as materials science, electronics, signal processing, computing and manufacturing. They are a perfect combination of the latest achievements of many disciplines.

Biomedical ultrasonics keeps developing and maturing, and its applications keep expanding, but the medical uses of ultrasound fall into two main areas: ultrasound diagnosis and ultrasound therapy.

Ultrasound diagnosis uses the information about biological tissue carried by the amplitude, frequency, phase and timing of ultrasound signals to measure, image and diagnose the human body. By measuring and imaging these parameters, ultrasound diagnosis picks up differences between tissues, characterizes them, and so diagnoses many organic and functional diseases.

When ultrasound energy acts on biological tissue, its mechanical, thermal and physicochemical effects raise the temperature of that tissue, improve blood circulation, boost metabolism, soften the tissue, change the pH, speed up chemical reactions and increase cell activity. These changes inevitably affect the functional state of that tissue, and through body fluids and nervous reflexes they also affect distant organs. The biological effects produced in irradiated tissues and cells depend directly on the intensity of the ultrasound and the exposure time. Ultrasound therapy exploits the body’s absorption of ultrasound, together with the biological effects of ultrasound and their mechanisms, to achieve its therapeutic goals.

How biomedical ultrasound systems are classified

By principle, purpose and equipment architecture, biomedical ultrasound systems can be divided broadly by use into two categories, diagnostic and therapeutic, as mentioned in the overview above. They can also be divided by other criteria into many more specific types, which makes them easier to understand. The classification goes as follows.

1. By waveform

As the name suggests, this classifies systems by the waveform the ultrasound probe emits. There are two main types, continuous-wave and pulsed:

1) Continuous-wave ultrasound devices

A continuous wave is present all the time, without interruption. Figure 8 shows two continuous waves of different wavelengths.

Figure 8. Continuous waves

2) Pulsed-wave ultrasound devices

Pulsed transmission and reception is the most widely used approach in medical ultrasound equipment for both treatment and diagnosis. A pulse is a short, interrupted signal that is discontinuous in time. It can occur singly or repeatedly, intermittently or periodically. Figure 9 shows a single pulse.

Figure 9. A single pulse

2. By physical method

The key distinction here is whether the system processes reflected or transmitted ultrasound signals. Again there are two main types, echo and transmission:

1) Echo (pulse-echo) ultrasound scanners

These extract the information they need for diagnosis from the echoes, that is, the reflected signals. Usually a single probe both transmits the ultrasound and receives the reflections, as shown in Figure 10.

Figure 10. How a pulse-echo ultrasound scanner works

2) Transmission ultrasound scanners

This was the earliest ultrasound diagnostic technique to be used. Much like X-ray imaging, it obtains the medical information it needs from ultrasound that has passed through biological tissue. Usually one probe transmits the ultrasound and a second probe receives the transmitted wave, as shown in Figure 11.

Figure 11. How a transmission ultrasound scanner works

3. By system architecture

Classifying by system architecture gives a much richer list. The “B-scan” mentioned above is in fact shorthand from this scheme: its full name is “B-mode ultrasound diagnostic scanner” or “B-mode ultrasound cross-sectional imager.” So how many kinds of medical ultrasound equipment are there under this scheme? We list eleven below. Biomedical ultrasound keeps evolving, though, so there are surely other kinds, and the list is for reference only. If you’re interested, read through the eleven types below, which describe roughly how each one works and where its name comes from. If you find it dry, just skim the names and skip to the videos at the end to relax. They give a rough idea of how ultrasound diagnosis and therapy work.

1) A-mode ultrasound scanners

A-mode is the most basic display mode. On the oscilloscope tube, the horizontal axis shows the travel time of the ultrasound, that is, the depth, and the vertical axis shows the amplitude of the echo pulses. Hence the name A-mode, for amplitude.

2) M-mode ultrasound scanners

Developed from the A-mode scanner, this is one of the most basic ultrasound diagnostic devices. Brightness on the display tube represents echo amplitude: the A-mode echo amplitude is applied to the tube’s Z-axis brightness-modulation electrode. The vertical axis shows the travel time of the ultrasound pulses, that is, the depth, and a slow time-base sweep voltage is applied to the horizontal deflection plates. Scanning the body thus produces a trace of how each echo-producing structure moves. The name M-mode comes from “motion.”

3) B-mode ultrasound scanners

The B-mode scanner is also called a B-mode cross-sectional imager. It uses the amplitude of the echo pulses to modulate the brightness of the display, while the horizontal and vertical axes of the display correspond point by point to the position of the scanning beam. The result is a brightness-modulated cross-sectional ultrasound image. The name B-mode comes from “brightness.”

4) Doppler ultrasound scanners

Doppler ultrasound scanners are also called D-mode, after Doppler. They detect moving targets using the Doppler effect caused by relative motion between the ultrasound and the target as the wave propagates.

5) C-mode and F-mode ultrasound imaging devices

Developed from the B-mode scanner, these acquire and image echo information on planes and curved surfaces that are perpendicular to the beam direction or at an angle to it.

6) Ultrasonic surgical devices

Ultrasonic surgery is a field of medical ultrasound that emerged after ultrasound therapy and diagnosis. It uses fairly intense ultrasound to break up diseased tissue in the eye or kidney and remove it, performing surgery with ultrasound.

7) Ultrasound therapy devices

These mainly exploit the tissue’s absorption of ultrasound energy and the resulting thermal, mechanical and chemical effects to treat disease.

8) Interventional ultrasound devices

Intracavitary ultrasound imaging developed in recent years includes transesophageal, transvaginal, transurethral, laparoscopic and intravascular ultrasound.

9) Ultrasound holography devices

Borrowing the concept from optical information processing, these use the interference and diffraction of two ultrasound beams to capture the amplitude and phase of the ultrasound, and then reconstruct the amplitude and phase with a laser.

10) Acoustic microscopes

An acoustic microscope is used to observe the fine structure, properties and changes of human tissues and cells.

11) Ultrasound CT

Ultrasound CT transplants and extends the theory of X-ray CT. Replacing the X-rays with an ultrasound beam and reconstructing an image from the transmission data, just as with X-rays, is called ultrasound CT.

Mingxi Wan, Yujin Zong and Supin Wang. Biomedical Ultrasonics [M] (in Chinese). Science Press, 2010.

The book covers every aspect of biomedical ultrasound in considerable detail, for anyone who wants to read further.
